title: Mediterranean Diet for Arthritis: A 14-Day UK Meal Plan
meta_title: Mediterranean Diet for Arthritis: A 14-Day UK Meal Plan
meta_description: A flexible 14-day UK Mediterranean-style meal plan, with honest NICE evidence limits, vegetarian swaps, fish guidance, food safety and small-appetite advice.

direct_answer: Mediterranean-style eating can support a balanced diet, but it does not replace arthritis treatment. NICE says there is no strong evidence that diet changes benefit rheumatoid arthritis, while encouraging Mediterranean principles. This flexible 14-day meal plan is not a prescribed diet or a promised symptom response.
author: Louis Maxwell
content:
Quick answer: Mediterranean-style eating can be a practical way to build a balanced diet, but it is not a treatment that reliably lowers arthritis inflammation or replaces medicines. NICE says there is no strong evidence that changing diet benefits rheumatoid arthritis, while encouraging Mediterranean principles. This flexible 14-day plan gives everyday meal ideas, not a prescribed diet or a promised symptom response.

What NICE says, and what research cannot promise

NICE NG100, recommendation 1.8.8, says adults with rheumatoid arthritis who want to experiment with diet should be told that there is no strong evidence their arthritis will benefit. It also says they can be encouraged to follow Mediterranean principles: more bread, fruit, vegetables and fish, less meat, and vegetable or plant oils in place of butter and cheese.

This is not a claim that all arthritis types respond to the same diet. Studies of Mediterranean-style eating in rheumatoid arthritis are small and differ in what participants eat, their medicines and the support they receive. Some report symptom improvements, but results are mixed and the size of a clinically useful benefit is uncertain. A change in an inflammatory blood marker does not by itself prove better joint outcomes.

The 2025 review of Mediterranean eating and rheumatoid arthritis describes these limits. There is no basis here to promise a fall in CRP, less need for anti-inflammatory medicine, or a response within six to eight weeks. Keep prescribed treatment and monitoring in place. Do not wait for a diet trial to seek help for new swelling or worsening symptoms.

How to use this plan

This is a set of meal ideas for adults who can eat a normal varied diet. It is not a calorie-controlled or weight-loss plan, and the portions are yours to adapt. Add snacks and enough food to meet your appetite, activity and health needs. A dietitian can help if you need a personalised plan.

Use the NHS Eatwell Guide across the day or week: vegetables and fruit, starchy foods such as bread, potatoes, rice and pasta, protein foods, dairy or suitable alternatives, and small amounts of unsaturated oils. Olive oil is a food, not an alternative to ibuprofen. You do not need an expensive brand or a supplement to follow the pattern.

These ideas include wheat, fish, eggs, milk, soya, nuts, seeds and sesame in some meals. Check every ingredient label and make suitable swaps for an allergy or intolerance. Do not follow this general plan unchanged if you have swallowing difficulties, coeliac disease, kidney disease, a prescribed special diet or other needs that affect what you can eat. Ask your clinician or dietitian.

Week 1: seven days of meals

Day 1

  • Breakfast: Porridge with milk or fortified soya drink, berries and walnuts
  • Lunch: Hummus and vegetable wholemeal wrap, with fruit
  • Dinner: Baked salmon, potatoes, broccoli and peas

Day 2

  • Breakfast: Egg or tofu scramble on wholemeal toast
  • Lunch: Lentil and vegetable soup with bread
  • Dinner: Chickpea, spinach and tomato stew with brown rice

Day 3

  • Breakfast: Plain yoghurt or fortified soya yoghurt, oats and banana
  • Lunch: Bean and pepper salad with a wholemeal roll
  • Dinner: Chicken or tofu traybake with courgettes, carrots and couscous

Day 4

  • Breakfast: Overnight oats with pear and seeds
  • Lunch: Baked potato with beans and salad
  • Dinner: Baked cod, roasted tomatoes and new potatoes

Day 5

  • Breakfast: Wholemeal toast with peanut butter or seed spread and banana
  • Lunch: Wholemeal pitta with hummus and grated carrot
  • Dinner: Lentil and mushroom bolognese with wholewheat pasta

Day 6

  • Breakfast: Porridge with apple and cinnamon
  • Lunch: Vegetable omelette or chickpea-flour pancake with salad
  • Dinner: Bean chilli with brown rice and yoghurt or fortified soya yoghurt

Day 7

  • Breakfast: Plain yoghurt or fortified soya yoghurt, berries and oats
  • Lunch: Tomato and butter-bean soup with bread
  • Dinner: Turkey or bean meatballs, wholewheat pasta and green vegetables

Week 2: another seven days

Day 8

  • Breakfast: Wholemeal toast with egg or calcium-set tofu and tomatoes
  • Lunch: Chickpea and cucumber pitta with fruit
  • Dinner: Baked salmon, couscous and mixed vegetables

Day 9

  • Breakfast: Porridge with pear and pumpkin seeds
  • Lunch: Lentil soup with bread and a small portion of cheese or hummus
  • Dinner: Vegetable and chickpea curry with brown rice

Day 10

  • Breakfast: Plain yoghurt or fortified soya yoghurt with banana and oats
  • Lunch: Wholemeal bean and avocado wrap
  • Dinner: Chicken or tofu stir-fry with vegetables and brown rice

Day 11

  • Breakfast: Wholemeal toast with beans
  • Lunch: Baked potato with hummus and salad
  • Dinner: Cod and tomato stew with potatoes and green vegetables

Day 12

  • Breakfast: Overnight oats with berries and peanut butter or seed spread
  • Lunch: Lentil and pepper salad with bread
  • Dinner: Aubergine and chickpea traybake with couscous

Day 13

  • Breakfast: Egg or tofu scramble on toast
  • Lunch: Tomato and white-bean soup with a wholemeal roll
  • Dinner: Vegetable and bean shepherd's pie with peas

Day 14

  • Breakfast: Porridge with milk or fortified soya drink, apple and walnuts
  • Lunch: Hummus, cucumber and tomato wholemeal sandwich
  • Dinner: Roast chicken or lentil loaf, potatoes, carrots and greens

Fish, vegetarian and vegan swaps

The plan offers one oily-fish meal and one white-fish meal in each week. The NHS fish guide recommends at least two portions a week, including one oily fish, for a balanced diet. It also gives limits and extra advice for pregnancy, breastfeeding and children. Follow that advice rather than adding extra oily fish every day. Tuna does not count as oily fish.

If you do not eat fish or meat, use beans, lentils, chickpeas or tofu as the protein part of the meal. A plant-based version still needs planning. Choose suitable fortified alternatives and make sure you have reliable sources of vitamin B12, calcium, iodine and other nutrients. The NHS vegan diet guide explains this. Check that a plant drink or yoghurt is fortified; products vary.

Make shopping and cooking easier on painful hands

Choose foods you can afford and prepare: tinned beans and lentils, frozen vegetables, plain frozen fish, oats, potatoes and wholemeal bread can all fit. Frozen or tinned produce can count towards your fruit and vegetable intake. Compare prices and labels rather than assuming a food is cheaper or nutritionally identical in every form.

Use pre-chopped vegetables, a light pan, easy-open tins or a suitable tin opener if these help. Share preparation or use ready-prepared ingredients when needed. You do not have to cook every meal from scratch. Keep food you can manage for days when pain or fatigue is worse.

Batch cooking is optional. Follow the Food Standards Agency chilling and freezing guidance and the pack instructions. Cool cooked food promptly, refrigerate or freeze it safely, and do not leave a week's cooked meals in the fridge without checking their safe storage time. Rice and reheated foods need particular care; follow the relevant food-safety instructions.

If your appetite is small or you are losing weight

Eating enough matters more than following a label. If you are frail, underweight or losing weight without trying, do not cut down on food, fat or protein just to make this plan look healthier. Smaller, regular meals and snacks may be easier. Tell your GP about unintentional weight loss and ask for dietetic help. See NHS malnutrition advice.

Drinks, supplements and checking whether a change helps

The NHS guide of six to eight cups or glasses of fluid a day is a general guide, not a target for everyone. Follow any fluid limit or other advice from your healthcare team. Water, milk and other suitable drinks can count. See NHS hydration advice.

This plan does not require turmeric capsules, fish-oil capsules, collagen, a special oil or any other arthritis supplement. Food ingredients are not the same as concentrated extracts. Ask a pharmacist before starting a supplement, especially if you take blood thinners or other prescribed medicines. Do not change a medicine dose because of a food claim.

If you want to record how you feel, note meals alongside pain, stiffness, sleep and any treatment changes, without treating a diary as proof of cause. Symptoms can change for many reasons. There is no validated two-week or six-to-eight-week deadline in the sources here for deciding that this plan has treated arthritis. Review what is practical and enjoyable, and discuss persistent symptoms with your team.

When to get medical help

Ask for an urgent GP appointment or get help from NHS 111 for sudden severe joint pain or a newly hot or swollen joint, even without fever. Do not assume it is a diet reaction or your usual arthritis. In Northern Ireland use your GP or GP out-of-hours service. A joint infection needs prompt treatment.

Call 999 for severe breathing difficulty, sudden confusion, or sudden chest pain that does not go away, spreads to an arm, neck or jaw, or comes with sweating, sickness, light-headedness or breathlessness. Call 999 or go to A&E for back pain with pain, tingling, weakness or numbness in both legs, loss of feeling around the genitals or anus, or new bladder, bowel or sexual-function changes. Do not drive yourself.

Arrange a review for persistent swelling, unexplained weight loss, or pain and fatigue that affect your daily life. Do not wait for the fortnight to end. Ask your GP about a dietitian if food restriction, cost, appetite or a medical diet makes eating difficult.
